summary: The Khawarij were an early deviant sect that arose during the First Fitna (civil war) and is condemned in prophetic hadith for their practice of declaring Muslims who commit major sins to be disbelievers (kafir) and their justification of killing them. They are the prototype of takfiri extremism in Islamic history.
overview:
The Khawarij (Arabic: al-Khawarij, meaning 'those who exited' or 'those who went out') emerged during the First Fitna — the civil war following the assassination of Caliph Uthman ibn Affan (d. 35 AH / 656 CE). They originally supported Ali ibn Abi Talib but turned against him when he agreed to arbitration with Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan at the Battle of Siffin (37 AH / 657 CE). Their slogan — 'Judgment belongs to Allah alone (la hukma illa lillah)' — expressed their rejection of human arbitration in what they considered a clear religious matter. Ali famously responded: 'A true statement used to express falsehood.'

The defining theological position of the Khawarij is the takfir (declaration of apostasy) of Muslims who commit major sins — making them liable to be fought and killed. This was a radical departure from the mainstream Sunni position, which holds that a Muslim who commits a major sin remains a Muslim and is accountable to Allah on the Day of Judgment.

The Prophet ﷺ warned about this group in numerous hadith. In Sahih al-Bukhari (No. 6163) and Sahih Muslim (No. 1066), he described 'a group that will recite the Quran but it will not pass beyond their throats' and said they 'will exit the religion as an arrow exits its target.' He called for them to be fought wherever they are found.

The first Khawarij group was defeated militarily by Ali at the Battle of Nahrawan (38 AH / 658 CE). However, Khawarij ideology resurfaced in various forms throughout Islamic history. A surviving branch, the Ibadis (considered distinct from the classical Khawarij by most contemporary scholars), became established in Oman.

The Prophet's description of the Khawarij — their outward religious devotion combined with their extremism — was applied by classical scholars, including Ibn Taymiyyah, to later groups that practiced mass takfir and violence against Muslims. Modern manifestations of this pattern — declaring Muslim rulers, scholars, or populations kafir and using this as justification for violence — are condemned under the same Khawarij rubric by mainstream Sunni scholars.
disclaimer_note: The Khawarij are condemned by name in prophetic hadith (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim) for their practice of declaring Muslims kafir for sins and fighting them. They are the historical prototype for takfiri extremism. Modern groups that practice mass takfir and justify violence against Muslims are evaluated against this same standard by mainstream Sunni scholars.
